label: Riverside
rationale: The ambitious large-ensemble peak of Yusef Lateef's Riverside period: his largest group to date (a nine-piece with three brass, three reeds including bassoon, and three rhythm) playing an expanded book — his own compositions beside two ambitious pieces by classical composer Charles Mills and the first recorded writing (arrangement and the tune 'Revelation') by a then-teenaged Kenny Barron, predating Barron's debut as a player. DownBeat 4.5 stars (Don DeMicheal: 'The album is a mature statement by a mature artist'); AllMusic 4 stars (Proefrock: 'an album that bursts with new ideas and textures, while remaining accessible, and above all, beautiful'); cited in The Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings. Session gravity is strong: Clark Terry, Curtis Fuller, Richard Williams, Tate Houston, and the then-unknown Joe Zawinul in the same room with Lateef's oboe, arghul and flute. Second Lateef contribution alongside Eastern Sounds (1961) — a different statement, not a duplicate: where Eastern Sounds is the intimate late-night classic, this is the orchestral/world-music experiment, and the direct predecessor that made Eastern Sounds possible.
scope_flag: World-music-inflected hard bop on the modal seam — inside the 1940-1979 window and the hard-bop tradition, but the unusual instrumentation (oboe, bassoon, arghul, tambourine-adjacent percussion) and Charles Mills's classical-leaning pieces put it at the edge of the canon's center of gravity.

personnel_record.notes: Three sessions. October 4 and 6, 1960, Plaza Sound Studios, NYC (original LP, Riverside RLP 337): full nine-piece — Lateef, Williams, Terry, Fuller, Taylor, Houston, Zawinul, Tucker, Humphries. June 23, 1961, Bell Sound Studios, NYC: quintet-plus-percussion date (Lateef, Harris, Farrow, Humphries, Masseaux, Sanders, plus unidentified background voices) whose two tracks were originally released only as a 45-RPM single and appear on the album as CD-era bonus tracks. Track-to-session split for the two October dates is an inference from LP side order and standard discographic practice; JazzDisco gives one roster for both dates without per-track assignment — hence track_assignments_complete: false. CONFLICTS PRESERVED: (1) Personnel — AllMusic and Concord merge the 1961 bonus-session musicians (Barry Harris, Ernie Farrow, Garvin Masseaux, Roger Sanders) into the album's credits; the JazzDisco sessionography and the original LP rear cover restrict them to the two bonus tracks. Both claims recorded; bonus-session players scoped to tracks 8-9. (2) Producer — Wikipedia infobox and AllMusic give Orrin Keepnews; AllMusic also credits John Levy (most plausibly the 45 single producer); Keepnews recorded as primary, Levy noted. (3) Engineer — Discogs and AllMusic list Ray Fowler; AllMusic also lists Bill Stoddard; per-session coverage undetermined, both recorded. (4) Release year — AllMusic dates the release 1961; Discogs, Wikipedia, Concord and iTunes give 1960 (Riverside RLP 337); 1960 retained. (5) Durations — Wikipedia/AllMusic CD timings used; Discogs LP timings run ~9-11 seconds shorter per track (e.g. Revelation 5:53, Apathy 5:20). (6) Clark Terry doubling — JazzDisco lists trumpet, Wikipedia flugelhorn and trumpet; treated as doubling, not resolved. Taxonomy gaps: oboe, argol (arghul), bassoon are not in the instrument taxonomy. Name pseudonym: 'Roger Sanders' = Montego Joe (JazzDisco). Kenny Barron appears as composer ('Revelation') and arranger ('Ev'ry Day') but not as a player. Ken Deardoff cover design, Lawrence Shustak photography, Chris Albertson liner notes (CD), Gary Hobish remastering (AllMusic). Second Yusef Lateef candidate — Eastern Sounds (1961) is already in the canon and this is a distinct album, not a duplicate.

ballot.album: Yusef Lateef — The Centaur and the Phoenix (1960)
ballot.case_for: The session gravity is the strongest signal: a nine-piece Riverside date with Clark Terry, Curtis Fuller, Richard Williams, and Tate Houston — and, crucially, a then-unknown Joe Zawinul on piano alongside the first recorded writing and arranging by a teenaged Kenny Barron ('Revelation,' 'Ev'ry Day'). DownBeat's 4.5-star contemporary review (DeMicheal: 'a mature statement by a mature artist') and AllMusic's 4 stars (Proefrock: 'bursts with new ideas and textures, while remaining accessible, and above all, beautiful') mark it as a recognized statement of Lateef's large-ensemble/world-music-inflected hard-bop vision, distinct from the intimate Eastern Sounds and prior to it in the discography.
ballot.case_against: The consensus claim is thinner than it first appears — the Penguin Guide is cited but no star rating or core-collection designation is quoted, and no NPR, JazzTimes, or DownBeat canon-list presence is surfaced, so the for-case rests on a single contemporary review plus standard AllMusic metadata. The discovery test cuts against it too: the Charles Mills classical-leaning pieces and the heterogeneous instrumentation (oboe, bassoon, arghul) make the album feel more like a fascinating transitional experiment than a unified, load-bearing canonical statement, and Eastern Sounds already occupies the Lateef slot a curious listener is sent to. The 1961 Bell Sound bonus session, with its own rhythm section (Harris, Farrow), is a packaging artifact rather than a coherent artistic whole — six unresolved conflicts in the dossier (personnel merge, producer, engineer, release year) confirm the record's boundaries are messier than the 'large-ensemble peak' framing admits.
ballot.disagreement: Both references agree on the tier (contested) and priority (consider); the split is a genuine emphasis difference — Reference 1 leans harder on the thinness of the editorial consensus (Penguin Guide uncharacterized, no canon-list presence) as the leading against-case, while Reference 2 leads with the discovery test and the album's transitional, third-stream-adjacent feel. Both are real; the ballot preserves both.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John hold this at contested/consider: the Zawinul-and-Barron lineage case is strong enough to keep alive, but the canonical weight is not yet clear enough to promote — listen to it against Eastern Sounds and decide whether the large-ensemble/world-music experiment earns a second Lateef slot or whether the personnel history alone justifies it.
